newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish markets take NBP rate rise talk as warning.
newsitem.headline: Polish markets take NBP rate rise talk as warning.

text.p: Polish T-bill yields firmed on the central banker's Wednesday statement on a possible rate rise, but analysts saw it more as a warning to banks to keep credit under control than a threat of immediate action.

Central bank president Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz was quoted by Poland's biggest newspaper as saying at the annual International Monterary Fund/World Bank meeting in Washington that rates might go up to counter a recent boom in credit action.
The Gazeta Wyborcza daily reported Gronkiewicz-Waltz also said the rapid rise in lending could lead to an increase of bad credits and push the Polish banking system back into a bad loans crisis.
But banking analysts said this was not likely to happen.
"This is a serious warning for banks to be cautious when giving credit," said Stanislaw Pietrasiewicz, the head of the credit department at Poland's largest savings bank PKO BP.
Analysts said the increase in credit action would inevitably lead to more bad-credits, but that their ratio to the whole credit portfolio was unlikely to rise significantly.
They said that if Poland's economic growth slows, then more loans will probably not be repaid in time, but that the banking system would not fall into bad-credit crisis as in 1991.
Lending to the non-financial sector rose 2.8 percent in the first 20 days of September after rising four percent in August.
Since the start of the year it has increased by 24 percent against a 17.4 percent rise in broad money supply.

The central bank last cut official interest rates by one percentage point to 25 and 22 percent on July 16, but most analysts said that the NBP would likely refrain from a rate move in the near future.

"The possibility of an interest rate rise exsists, but I don't expect the central bank will touch interest rates within the next month-and-a-half," said Andrzej Ladko, senior dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.

Analysts said the seasonal rise of food prices after harvest, October's five percent rise in utility prices and the expected increases in gasoline prices after Poland lifts price controls on fuels would likely keep inflation from falling in the next months making a rate cut unlikely.

Polish T-bill yields and longer-term deposits rose slightly on Thursday in reaction to Gronkiewicz-Waltz's statement, as analysts, who earlier expected the central bank to pare rates in the near-term, priced-in a possible interest rate rise.
"Today's reaction was mainly psychological -- after the Gronkiewicz-Waltz statement T-bill yields rose in secondary trade," said Andzej Kopec, chief dealer at Bank Slaski SA.
